claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: IC neurons exhibit selective responses to the spectral and temporal content of sounds.
claims.source: Neurons in the IC exhibit selective responses to the spectral and temporal content of sounds and perform computations important for sound localization and the identification of speech and other communication sounds (Felix et al., 2018; Winer and Schreiner, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: IC neurons have disc-shaped or stellate morphologies.
claims.source: Anatomical studies have shown that IC neurons have disc-shaped or stellate morphologies (Malmierca et al., 1993; Meininger et al., 1986; Oliver and Morest, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Disc-shaped neurons maintain their dendritic arbors within isofrequency lamina.
claims.source: Disc-shaped neurons maintain their dendritic arbors within isofrequency lamina and make up the majority of neurons in the tonotopically organized central nucleus of the IC (ICc).
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Stellate neurons in the ICc extend their dendritic arbors across laminae.
claims.source: Stellate neurons in the ICc extend their dendritic arbors across laminae and are therefore thought to integrate information across sound frequencies (Oliver et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and represents an inference about function based on morphology.

claims.claim: Both disc-shaped and stellate cells can be glutamatergic or GABAergic.
claims.source: Both disc-shaped and stellate cells can be glutamatergic or GABAergic, an indication that each of these morphological groups consists of at least two neuron types (Oliver et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: IC GABAergic neurons have been divided into four classes based on soma size and extracellular markers.
claims.source: Based on soma size and extracellular markers, IC GABAergic neurons have been divided into four classes (Beebe et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Large GABAergic neurons are the one consistently identified neuron type in the IC.
claims.source: Among these, 'large GABAergic' neurons are the one consistently identified neuron type in the IC (Geis and Borst, 2013; Ito et al., 2015; Ito et al., 2009; Ito and Oliver, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: There are currently no known molecular markers specific for large GABAergic neurons.
claims.source: However, there are currently no known molecular markers specific for large GABAergic neurons (Schofield and Beebe, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous review.

claims.claim: IC neuron responses to tones form a continuum and cannot be used alone to define functionally significant groups.
claims.source: IC neurons exhibit diverse responses to tones, but a comprehensive study showed that these responses form a continuum and cannot be used on their own to define functionally significant groups of neurons (Palmer et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Disc-shaped neurons could not be divided into distinct groups by matching their morphology with their in vivo physiology.
claims.source: In addition, disc-shaped neurons could not be divided into distinct groups by matching their morphology with their in vivo physiology (Wallace et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: GABAergic and glutamatergic IC neurons exhibit overlapping and equally diverse responses to sounds.
claims.source: Similarly, GABAergic and glutamatergic IC neurons exhibit overlapping and equally diverse responses to sounds (Ono et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: IC neuron firing patterns do not correlate with neuronal morphology or neurotransmitter phenotype.
claims.source: In vitro recordings have shown that IC neurons exhibit diverse firing patterns, but these firing patterns do not correlate with neuronal morphology or neurotransmitter phenotype (Ono et al., 2005; Peruzzi et al., 2000; Reetz and Ehret, 1999; Sivaramakrishnan and Oliver, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: VIP-expressing neurons in VIP-IRES-Cre x Ai14 mice expressed the fluorescent protein tdTomato.
claims.source: By crossing VIP-IRES-Cre mice with Ai14 reporter mice, we obtained mice in which VIP+ neurons expressed the fluorescent protein tdTomato.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach used in the study.

claims.claim: Distribution of VIP+ neurons throughout the brain matched the description provided by Taniguchi et al. (2011).
claims.source: Distribution of VIP+ neurons throughout the brain matched the description provided by Taniguchi et al. (2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison to a previous study.

claims.claim: There were very few or no VIP-expressing neurons in auditory centers outside of the IC, with the exception of auditory cortex.
claims.source: There were very few or no VIP-expressing neurons in auditory centers outside of the IC (including cochlear nucleus, superior olivary complex, nuclei of the lateral lemniscus, nucleus of the brachium of the IC and medial geniculate nucleus), with the exception of auditory cortex, where sparse neurons matching descriptions of VIP-expressing interneurons were labeled.
claims.evidence: This is based on observations from the VIP-IRES-Cre x Ai14 mice.

claims.claim: VIP+ neurons were present in the ICc, ICd, and IClc.
claims.source: Labeled neurons were present throughout most of the rostro-caudal extent of the IC, including in the ICc, ICd, and IClc, but were most numerous in the caudal regions.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claims.claim: VIP+ neurons were most numerous in the caudal regions of the IC.
claims.source: Labeled neurons were present throughout most of the rostro-caudal extent of the IC, including in the ICc, ICd, and IClc, but were most numerous in the caudal regions.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claims.claim: VIP+ neurons were rare or absent in the IC rostral pole and intercollicular tegmentum.
claims.source: Labeled neurons were rare or absent in the IC rostral pole and intercollicular tegmentum.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claims.claim: Only 1.3% of tdTomato+ neurons co-labeled with GAD67.
claims.source: Across 793 tdTomato+ neurons, only 10 neurons co-labeled with GAD67 (1.3%, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical analysis shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: VIP neurons are a subgroup of glutamatergic neurons in the ICc, ICd, and IClc.
claims.source: These data suggest that VIP neurons are a subgroup of glutamatergic neurons in the ICc, ICd, and IClc.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of GAD67 co-labeling in VIP neurons.

claims.claim: VIP neurons represent 3.5% of ICc neurons.
claims.source: The results of the stereological analysis revealed that VIP neurons represented a larger portion of neurons in the ICc (3.5 ± 1.0%) than in the IC shell (1.5 ± 0.2%; two-tailed t-test, t(79) = 2.86, p = 0.005; Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on stereological analysis using NeuN staining shown in Table 2.

claims.claim: VIP neurons represent 1.5% of IC shell neurons.
claims.source: The results of the stereological analysis revealed that VIP neurons represented a larger portion of neurons in the ICc (3.5 ± 1.0%) than in the IC shell (1.5 ± 0.2%; two-tailed t-test, t(79) = 2.86, p = 0.005; Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on stereological analysis using NeuN staining shown in Table 2.

claims.claim: The prevalence of VIP neurons was highest in caudal regions of the ICc and the IC shell.
claims.source: In addition, the prevalence of VIP neurons was highest in caudal regions of the ICc and the IC shell and tended to decrease in a caudal to rostral gradient.
claims.evidence: This is based on stereological analysis shown in Table 2.

claims.claim: VIP neurons represent 2.3% of the total population of neurons in the mouse IC.
claims.source: Overall, a combined count of VIP neurons from the ICc and IC shell showed that VIP neurons represent 2.3 ± 0.3% of the total population of neurons in the mouse IC (208 of 9304 neurons, n = 69 systematic random samples).
claims.evidence: This is based on stereological analysis combining ICc and IC shell data.

claims.claim: VIP neurons had a resting membrane potential of −69.5 mV ± 4.4 mV.
claims.source: VIP neurons had a resting membrane potential of −69.5 mV ± 4.4 mV (n = 216, corrected for liquid junction potential).
claims.evidence: This is based on whole cell patch clamp recordings.

claims.claim: VIP neurons showed minimal to no voltage sag to hyperpolarizing current steps.
claims.source: In response to a current step protocol with hyperpolarizing and depolarizing current injections, VIP neurons showed minimal to no voltage sag to hyperpolarizing current steps and a sustained firing pattern of action potentials to depolarizing current steps (Figure 3A1, A2).
claims.evidence: This is based on whole cell patch clamp recordings shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: 90.3% of patched VIP neurons exhibited a sustained firing pattern.
claims.source: 90.3% (214 of 237) of patched VIP neurons exhibited a sustained firing pattern, 8.4% (20 of 237) showed an adapting firing pattern (SFA ratio >= 2), and 1.3% (3 of 237) of VIP neurons had a transient firing pattern (firing stopped before the end of the current step).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of whole cell patch clamp recordings.

claims.claim: VIP neurons on average had a higher peak input resistance than non-targeted neurons.
claims.source: VIP neurons on average had a higher peak input resistance (Rpk) than non-targeted neurons (mean ± SD: VIP 242.1 ± 139.4 MΩ vs NT 191.1 ± 161.4 MΩ, p = 0.0003, Wilcoxon rank sum test)
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of electrophysiological properties between VIP and non-targeted neurons.

claims.claim: VIP neurons on average had a higher steady-state input resistance than non-targeted neurons.
claims.source: a higher steady-state input resistance (Rss) (mean ± SD: VIP 239.7 ± 170.7 MΩ vs NT 153.4 ± 153.2, p = 0.0001, Wilcoxon rank sum test)
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of electrophysiological properties between VIP and non-targeted neurons.

claims.claim: VIP neurons on average had a slower membrane time constant than non-targeted neurons.
claims.source: a slower membrane time constant (mean ± SD: VIP 15.0 ± 8.8 ms vs NT 9.7 ± 7.6 MΩ, p = 6.8*10−7, Wilcoxon rank sum test)
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of electrophysiological properties between VIP and non-targeted neurons.

claims.claim: VIP neurons on average had lower rheobase values than non-targeted neurons.
claims.source: lower rheobase values (mean ± SD: VIP 67.8 ± 96.2 pA vs NT 120.0 ± 100.9 pA, p = 0.013, Wilcoxon rank sum test)
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of electrophysiological properties between VIP and non-targeted neurons.

claims.claim: VIP neurons on average had a much less pronounced voltage sag than non-targeted neurons.
claims.source: and a much less pronounced voltage sag (mean ± SD: VIP 0.87 ± 0.16 vs NT 0.75 ± 0.21, p = 0.0003, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of electrophysiological properties between VIP and non-targeted neurons.

claims.claim: The SFA ratio of VIP neurons was tightly clustered at 1.47 ± 1.62.
claims.source: Most striking, the SFA ratio of VIP neurons was tightly clustered at 1.47 ± 1.62, whereas SFA of NT neurons showed a significantly higher value and spread (3.62 ± 5.43, mean ± SD, p = 2.07*10−7).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of electrophysiological properties between VIP and non-targeted neurons.

claims.claim: Approximately one quarter of the variability in sag ratios was explained by location in the ICc.
claims.source: Approximately one quarter of the variability in sag ratios was explained by location in the ICc (sag ratio at −91 mV: R = 0.536, R2adj = 0.262, p = 1.24×10−05, n = 60, Figure 4B4; sag ratio at −111 mV: R = 0.516, R2adj = 0.233, p = 0.0002, n = 47, Figure 4B5).
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between intrinsic physiology and neuron location shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: A significant but smaller portion of the variability in membrane time constant was explained by location in the ICc.
claims.source: A significant but smaller portion of the variability in membrane time constant was explained by location in the ICc (τ: R = 0.343, R2adj = 0.088, p = 0.007, n = 61; Figure 4B3).
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between intrinsic physiology and neuron location shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Nearly all (94.2%) VIP neurons had spiny dendrites.
claims.source: Nearly all (81/86 = 94.2%) VIP neurons had spiny dendrites (Figure 5A,B insets).
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of biocytin-filled neurons shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: 28% of neurons from non-targeted recordings had spiny dendrites.
claims.source: This contrasts sharply with the 28% (12 of 43 neurons) of neurons that had spiny dendrites in non-targeted recordings from C57BL/6J mice (Figure 5C)
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of biocytin-filled neurons shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: VIP neurons had on average five primary dendrites.
claims.source: On average, VIP neurons had five primary dendrites (mean ± SD: 4.77 ± 1.38) that spread out in all directions from the soma, consistent with a stellate morphology.
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of reconstructed neurons.

claims.claim: 93% of VIP neurons in the ICc had a length to width ratio <3, classifying them as stellate.
claims.source: Applying this classification to our sample, 93% of VIP neurons in the ICc (39 of 42 neurons) had a length to width ratio <3, therefore being classified as stellate (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological analysis using the classification scheme from Oliver et al., 1991, shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Only 17% of VIP neurons had their longest axis oriented within ± 15° of the 45° laminar plane.
claims.source: Only 17% of VIP neurons (7 of 42) had their longest axis oriented within ± 15° of the 45° laminar plane, indicating that the dendritic arbors of most VIP neurons (83%, 35 of 42) may be positioned to cross one or more isofrequency laminae in the ICc (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The dendritic arbors of 83% of ICc VIP neurons spread more than 100 µm perpendicular to the laminar plane.
claims.source: The dendritic arbors of 83% of ICc VIP neurons (35 of 42) spread more than 100 µm perpendicular to the laminar plane, and more than 36% (15 of 42) spread more than 200 µm across the laminar plane (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: VIP neurons account for approximately 18-23% of ICc stellate neurons.
claims.source: Previous estimates indicate that approximately 15 – 20% of ICc neurons are stellate (Oliver et al., 1991; Oliver and Morest, 1984). Since our stereological analysis showed that VIP neurons represent 3.5% of ICc neurons, our results indicate that VIP neurons account for ~18 – 23% of ICc stellate neurons.
claims.evidence: This is calculated based on the percentage of VIP neurons in the ICc and previous estimates of stellate neuron prevalence.

claims.claim: Neurons that expressed eGFP routinely co-expressed tdTomato, confirming VIP expression.
claims.source: Neurons that expressed eGFP routinely co-expressed tdTomato, confirming VIP expression by those neurons (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is based on viral tract tracing experiments shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: eGFP-labeled axons were present in the contralateral IC, medial geniculate body, and superior olivary complex.
claims.source: Labeled axons and boutons were found in numerous auditory nuclei, including the contralateral IC, medial geniculate body and superior olivary complex (Figure 6D–F).
claims.evidence: This is based on viral tract tracing experiments shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Additional targets of VIP neurons included the nucleus of the brachium of the IC, the periaqueductal gray, and the superior colliculus.
claims.source: Additional targets included the nucleus of the brachium of the IC, the periaqueductal gray, and the superior colliculus (not shown; details of termination patterns and terminal axon morphology will be described in a subsequent report).
claims.evidence: This is based on viral tract tracing experiments.

claims.claim: VIP+ IC neurons contribute to ascending, commissural and descending pathways from the IC.
claims.source: These data indicate that VIP+ IC neurons contribute to ascending, commissural and descending pathways from the IC.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the viral tract tracing data showing projections to multiple targets.

claims.claim: Blue light flashes elicited IPSPs in 6 out of 12 VIP neurons tested in the presence of AMPA and NMDA receptor antagonists.
claims.source: In the presence of AMPA and NMDA receptor antagonists (10 µM NBQX and 50 µM D-AP5, bath application), 2 – 5 ms flashes of blue light elicited IPSPs in 6 out of 12 neurons tested (Figure 7C, left).
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Commissural IPSPs were completely abolished by gabazine.
claims.source: IPSPs were completely abolished by the GABAA receptor antagonist gabazine (5 µM, Figure 7C, right; n = 6; amplitude, p = 0.006; rise time, p = 0.003; halfwidth, p = 0.001; membrane time constant, p = 0.003, paired t-test).
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments with pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Commissural IPSPs in ICc VIP neurons were small (−1.53 mV ± 0.96 mV) on average.
claims.source: On average (n = 6), commissural IPSPs in ICc VIP neurons were small (−1.53 mV ± 0.96 mV) and had moderate 10 – 90% rise times (7.8 ms ± 2.1 ms), halfwidths (15.1 ms ± 6.8 ms) and decay time constants (32.4 ms ± 17.0 ms) (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Blue light flashes elicited EPSPs in 11 out of 27 VIP neurons in the presence of GABAA and glycine receptor antagonists.
claims.source: We found that 2 – 5 ms flashes of blue light elicited EPSPs in 11 out of 27 neurons (Figure 7D, left).
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Commissural EPSPs in VIP neurons were small (1.52 mV ± 1.08 mV) on average.
claims.source: On average (n = 6), commissural EPSPs in VIP neurons were small (1.52 mV ± 1.08 mV) and had moderate 10 – 90% rise times (8.3 ms ± 4.3 ms), halfwidths (19.6 ms ± 7.6 ms) and decay time constants (43.5 ms ± 16.8 ms) (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: D-AP5 significantly reduced the halfwidth of commissural EPSPs.
claims.source: Adding the NMDA receptor antagonist D-AP5 to the bath significantly reduced the halfwidth of EPSPs (14.3 ms ± 4.7 ms, p = 0.006)
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments with pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The remainder of the commissural EPSP was completely blocked by NBQX.
claims.source: The remainder of the EPSP was completely blocked by the AMPA receptor antagonist NBQX (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments with pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: VIP neurons in the ICc receive excitatory and inhibitory synaptic input from the contralateral IC.
claims.source: Combined, the commissural CRACM experiments show that VIP neurons in the ICc receive excitatory and inhibitory synaptic input from the contralateral IC.
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The connection probability for inhibitory commissural projections was 50%.
claims.source: Surprisingly, although GABAergic neurons make up <= 20% of commissural projections (Hernández et al., 2006; Nakamoto et al., 2013), we found a higher connection probability for inhibitory commissural projections (50%; 6 out of 12 recordings performed in the presence of NBQX and D-AP5), than for excitatory connections (41%; 11 out of 27 recordings performed in the presence of gabazine and strychnine).
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments and comparison to previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Blue light flashes evoked EPSPs in 19 of 25 VIP neurons tested for DCN input.
claims.source: We found that 2–5 ms pulses of blue light elicited EPSPs in 19 of 25 neurons tested, confirming that ICc VIP neurons receive synaptic input from the DCN.
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: DCN-evoked EPSPs had moderate amplitudes (2.85 mV ± 2.98 mV) on average.
claims.source: Light-evoked EPSPs had moderate amplitudes (2.85 mV ± 2.98 mV) and relatively slow rise times (4.2 ms ± 1.3 ms), halfwidths (20.6 ms ± 14.4 ms) and decay time constants (22.0 ms ± 6.7 ms) (n = 6 cells, Figure 8B, left and 8C).
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: D-AP5 had no significant effect on DCN-evoked EPSP properties.
claims.source: Interestingly, D-AP5 had no significant effect on any of the measured properties (amplitude: 2.80 mV ± 2.54 mV, p = 0.96, rise time: 4.4 ms ± 1.7 ms, p = 0.95, halfwidth: 15.4 ms ± 6.1 ms, p = 0.37, decay time constant: 29.0 ms ± 7.1 ms, p = 0.16, two tailed t-test, critical p value with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons = 0.0125) (Figure 8B, middle, and 8C).
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments with pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: NBQX completely abolished DCN-evoked EPSPs.
claims.source: Subsequent addition of NBQX completely abolished DCN-evoked EPSPs (Figure 8B, right), confirming that DCN synapses activate AMPA receptors on ICc VIP neurons.
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments with pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: EPSPs elicited by blue light flashes were completely and reversibly abolished by TTX in 3 of 3 tested VIP neurons.
claims.source: After TTX wash-in, EPSPs elicited by blue light flashes were completely and reversibly abolished in 3 of 3 tested VIP neurons (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments with TTX to test for action potential dependence.

claims.claim: 8 out of 12 non-VIP neurons received input from the DCN.
claims.source: We found that 8 out of 12 non-VIP neurons received input from the DCN.
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments in non-VIP neurons.

claims.claim: An IPSP was elicited 2–3 ms after the onset of the light-evoked EPSP in DCN-CRACM experiments without inhibitory receptor antagonists.
claims.source: Under these conditions, we observed that an IPSP was elicited 2–3 ms after the onset of the light-evoked EPSP (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Washing in gabazine restored the EPSP to values comparable to EPSPs recorded in the presence of inhibitory receptor antagonists.
claims.source: Washing in gabazine restored the EPSP to values comparable to the EPSPs recorded in the presence of inhibitory receptor antagonists (compare Figure 8B,C).
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments with pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: The IPSP significantly shortened the halfwidth of the elicited EPSP across five ICc VIP neurons.
claims.source: Across five ICc VIP neurons, the IPSP significantly shortened the halfwidth of the elicited EPSP (p = 0.048, paired t-test, Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Halfwidth reductions due to feedforward inhibition ranged from 22% to 73%, with a median reduction of 36%.
claims.source: Halfwidth reductions ranged from 22% to 73%, with a median reduction of 36%.
claims.evidence: This is based on CRACM experiments shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Ascending input from the DCN activates a feedforward inhibitory circuit within the IC.
claims.source: Thus, these results indicate that ascending input from the DCN activates a feedforward inhibitory circuit within the IC and that this circuit regulates the duration of DCN-evoked excitation in ICc VIP neurons.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the CRACM experiments showing disynaptic inhibition.

claims.claim: VIP neurons are well-positioned to influence auditory computations in a number of brain regions.
claims.source: Thus, VIP neurons are well-positioned to influence auditory computations in a number of brain regions.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the projection patterns and input sources of VIP neurons.

claims.claim: The identification of VIP neurons revealed that a molecularly-defined class of IC neurons can broadcast the output of the IC to multiple auditory and non-auditory brain regions.
claims.source: Surprisingly, the identification of VIP neurons revealed that a molecularly-defined class of IC neurons can broadcast the output of the IC to multiple auditory and non-auditory brain regions (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This is based on the viral tract tracing data showing projections to multiple targets.

claims.claim: Feedforward inhibitory circuits within the IC may regulate the temporal summation of ascending inputs.
claims.source: Input from the DCN also drove feedforward inhibition that could sculpt the effects of excitatory inputs to VIP neurons. Thus, feedforward inhibitory circuits within the IC may regulate the temporal summation of ascending inputs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the CRACM experiments showing feedforward inhibition.

claims.claim: VIP neurons are well-positioned to broadly influence auditory computations in numerous brain regions.
claims.source: By integrating multiple sources of input and participating in most of the major projections from the IC, VIP neurons are well-positioned to broadly influence auditory computations in numerous brain regions.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combination of input and output connectivity data.

claims.claim: A multifaceted classification scheme including molecular markers has enabled investigations into how specific classes of interneurons shape circuit computations in the cerebral cortex.
claims.source: In the cerebral cortex, a multifaceted classification scheme including molecular markers has enabled investigations into how specific classes of interneurons shape circuit computations, sensory processing, and animal behavior (Cichon et al., 2017; Kato et al., 2017; Kato et al., 2015; Kuchibhotla et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2013; Milstein et al., 2015; Pfeffer et al., 2013; Pi et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in cortex.

claims.claim: Tonotopic variation in the intrinsic physiology of VIP neurons was consistent with VIP neurons having faster membrane properties in lower frequency regions of the ICc.
claims.source: Tonotopic variation in the intrinsic physiology of VIP neurons was consistent with VIP neurons having faster membrane properties and therefore better temporal coding potential in lower frequency regions of the ICc.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation analysis between intrinsic physiology and location.

claims.claim: VIP neurons are not the only stellate neurons in the IC.
claims.source: It is important to note that it would not be possible to identify VIP neurons based on their morphology or physiology alone. VIP neurons are not the only stellate neurons in the IC, nor are they the only neurons with sustained firing patterns or dendritic spines.
claims.evidence: This is based on knowledge of IC neuron diversity from previous studies.

claims.claim: A multidimensional approach incorporating molecular markers will be essential to identifying the remaining neuron classes in the IC.
claims.source: We propose that a multidimensional approach incorporating molecular markers will be essential to identifying the remaining neuron classes in the IC.
claims.evidence: This is a proposal based on the success of the current study and challenges in previous studies.

claims.claim: IC cells that project to the contralateral thalamus commonly have a collateral projection to the ipsilateral thalamus.
claims.source: Previous retrograde labeling studies suggest that some patterns of collateral projection are more common than others for IC cells. IC cells that project to the contralateral thalamus appear to quite commonly have a collateral projection to the ipsilateral thalamus (Mellott et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Very few IC neurons project to the thalamus and the cochlear nucleus.
claims.source: In contrast, very few IC neurons project to the thalamus and the cochlear nucleus (Coomes and Schofield, 2004; Hashikawa and Kawamura, 1983; Okoyama et al., 2006)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Retrograde tracing studies underestimate collateral projections.
claims.source: Because retrograde tracing studies underestimate collateral projections (Schofield et al., 2007), such studies may have missed VIP neurons with collateral projections.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Excitatory postsynaptic responses in IC neurons often involve activation of NMDA receptors.
claims.source: Excitatory postsynaptic responses in IC neurons often involve activation of NMDA receptors (Ma et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Under in vivo conditions, the activation of NMDA receptors can influence how IC neurons respond to tones.
claims.source: Under in vivo conditions, the activation of NMDA receptors can influence how IC neurons respond to tones (Sanchez et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: In many brain regions, feedforward inhibitory circuits control the time window for temporal integration of synaptic input.
claims.source: In many brain regions, feedforward inhibitory circuits control the time window for temporal integration of synaptic input (Gabernet et al., 2005; Pouille and Scanziani, 2001; Roberts et al., 2013; Stokes and Isaacson, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: GABAergic neurons in the ICc provide local inhibitory input mainly to neurons in the same isofrequency lamina.
claims.source: In the ICc, it was recently shown that GABAergic neurons provide local inhibitory input mainly to neurons in the same isofrequency lamina (Sturm et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Ascending projections from most auditory brainstem nuclei restrict their synapses to subregions of the ICc.
claims.source: Ascending projections from most auditory brainstem nuclei restrict their synapses to subregions of the ICc, dividing the ICc into functional zones that may be specialized for processing specific classes of auditory cues (Brunso-Bechtold et al., 1981; Cant, 2013; Cant and Benson, 2006; Loftus et al., 2010; Oliver, 2005; Oliver et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: The distribution of VIP neurons overlaps with the monaural domain of the ICc.
claims.source: Intriguingly, this distribution overlaps with the monaural domain of the ICc, an area that predominantly receives input from monaural nuclei, including the contralateral DCN and AVCN and the ipsilateral ventral nucleus of the lateral lemniscus (VNLL) (Cant and Benson, 2006; Loftus et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of VIP neuron distribution to known anatomical organization of the ICc.

claims.claim: Excitatory ICc neurons that receive input from the DCN are unlikely to receive input from other ascending auditory sources.
claims.source: In addition, a recent study in mice showed that excitatory ICc neurons that receive input from the DCN are unlikely to receive input from other ascending auditory sources but likely to receive input from the ipsilateral auditory cortex (Chen et al., 2018).

claims.claim: VIP neurons are specialized for processing monaural cues, particularly from the DCN.

results.result: VIP neurons are a novel, molecularly-defined class of glutamatergic stellate neurons in the IC with sustained firing patterns. They represent 3.5% of ICc neurons, 1.5% of IC shell neurons, and approximately 18-23% of ICc stellate neurons. VIP neurons exhibit distinct electrophysiological properties including sustained firing (90.3% of neurons), higher input resistance, slower membrane time constants, lower rheobase, less voltage sag, and tightly clustered spike frequency adaptation ratios compared to non-targeted IC neurons. Morphologically, 94.2% have spiny dendrites, 93% are classified as stellate based on length-to-width ratios, and 83% have dendritic arbors extending >100 µm perpendicular to isofrequency laminae.
results.evaluation: This result is well-supported by converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches. The molecular identity is established through the VIP-IRES-Cre x Ai14 mouse line (C21), glutamatergic phenotype confirmed by GAD67 immunostaining showing only 1.3% co-labeling (C27, C28), stereological quantification provides population estimates (C29, C30, C32), comprehensive electrophysiological characterization demonstrates distinct properties with appropriate statistical comparisons (C33-C41), and detailed morphological reconstructions establish stellate identity with spiny dendrites (C44-C49). The calculation that VIP neurons represent 18-23% of stellate neurons is appropriately derived from combining current data with prior literature estimates (C50).

results.result: VIP neurons are distributed throughout the ICc, ICd, and IClc, with highest prevalence in caudal regions of the ICc and IC shell. This distribution overlaps with the monaural domain of the ICc, which receives input from monaural brainstem nuclei including the contralateral DCN.
results.evaluation: The distribution pattern is well-documented through immunohistochemistry and stereological analysis (C24-C26, C31). The caudal-to-rostral gradient is statistically significant for ICc (p=0.001) and IC shell (p=0.03). The overlap with the monaural domain (C91) is appropriately inferred by comparing VIP neuron distribution to known anatomical organization from cited literature, though this remains correlative rather than functionally demonstrated.

results.result: The intrinsic physiology of VIP neurons varies along the tonotopic axis of the ICc, with approximately 25% of variability in voltage sag ratios explained by location. This variation is consistent with VIP neurons having faster membrane properties in lower frequency (dorsolateral) regions of the ICc.
results.evaluation: The correlation analysis is appropriately conducted using plane fitting to 2D coordinates with proper statistical assessment (C42: R²=0.262, p=1.24×10⁻⁵ for sag ratio at -91 mV; C43: R²=0.088, p=0.007 for membrane time constant). The interpretation that faster properties occur in lower frequency regions (C80) is a reasonable inference based on the tonotopic organization of the ICc, though the functional implications remain speculative. Sample size (n=60-61 neurons) is adequate for this analysis.

results.result: VIP neurons project to multiple auditory and non-auditory targets including the medial geniculate body, contralateral IC, superior olivary complex, nucleus of the brachium of the IC, periaqueductal gray, and superior colliculus, indicating that a single molecularly-defined class of IC neurons can broadcast output to multiple brain regions via ascending, commissural, and descending pathways.
results.evaluation: The projection patterns are well-documented using Cre-dependent AAV viral tracing with appropriate controls confirming VIP identity through tdTomato co-expression (C51). Multiple target regions are clearly identified with anatomical evidence (C52, C53). The conclusion that VIP neurons contribute to multiple projection pathways (C54, C76) is appropriately supported, though the manuscript acknowledges that whether individual VIP neurons project to multiple targets versus representing distinct subpopulations remains to be determined. This is a significant finding as it reveals unexpected anatomical organization.

results.result: VIP neurons in the ICc receive both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic input from the contralateral IC. Commissural EPSPs are mediated by AMPA and NMDA receptors, while IPSPs are GABAergic. The connection probability for inhibitory commissural projections (50%) was higher than for excitatory connections (41%), despite GABAergic neurons comprising ≤20% of commissural projections.
results.evaluation: The CRACM experiments provide direct evidence for commissural connectivity with appropriate pharmacological controls to isolate excitatory and inhibitory components (C55-C61). The characterization of receptor subtypes is thorough with sequential antagonist application. The observation of higher inhibitory connection probability (C63) is surprising given anatomical estimates but is appropriately noted as such. Connection probabilities may be underestimates due to incomplete viral transfection. The use of TTX controls (mentioned for DCN inputs) supports that responses are synaptically mediated. Sample sizes are adequate (6-27 neurons depending on condition).

results.result: VIP neurons in the ICc receive excitatory synaptic input from the dorsal cochlear nucleus (DCN) with a connection probability of 76% (19/25 neurons). DCN-evoked EPSPs are mediated by AMPA receptors but not NMDA receptors under resting conditions, have moderate amplitudes (2.85 ± 2.98 mV) and relatively slow kinetics. Non-VIP neurons also receive DCN input (67%, 8/12 neurons) with similar properties.
results.evaluation: The CRACM experiments demonstrate DCN input with appropriate controls including TTX to confirm action potential dependence (C68). The pharmacological dissection clearly shows AMPA receptor mediation without significant NMDA receptor contribution (C66, C67), which is appropriately noted as differing from commissural inputs. The high connection probability (76%) is consistent with anatomical predictions. Comparison with non-VIP neurons (C69) provides important context, though the trend toward less variable kinetics in VIP neurons (mentioned in text) is not statistically significant. The interpretation that slow kinetics suggest temporal summation is reasonable but remains to be functionally tested.

results.result: Ascending input from the DCN drives feedforward inhibition to VIP neurons within the IC, significantly reducing EPSP halfwidth by 22-73% (median 36%). This disynaptic inhibitory circuit regulates the temporal integration of DCN-evoked excitation in VIP neurons.
results.evaluation: The feedforward inhibition is convincingly demonstrated through CRACM experiments without inhibitory blockers showing disynaptic IPSPs (C70) that are reversed by gabazine (C71). The quantification of EPSP halfwidth reduction is statistically significant (p=0.048, n=5) with substantial effect sizes (C72, C73). The interpretation that this represents a local feedforward circuit (C74) is well-supported by the latency (2-3 ms after EPSP onset) and the absence of ascending GABAergic projections in the slice preparation. This represents a novel circuit motif in the IC. However, the identity of the GABAergic interneurons providing feedforward inhibition remains unknown.

results.result: VIP neurons are well-positioned to influence auditory computations in multiple brain regions by integrating inputs from the contralateral IC and DCN and projecting to numerous targets. The authors hypothesize that VIP neurons are specialized for processing monaural cues, particularly from the DCN.
results.evaluation: While the anatomical and connectivity data support that VIP neurons could influence multiple brain regions (C75, C78), the actual functional impact remains to be demonstrated. The hypothesis about monaural specialization (C93) is reasonable given the distribution overlapping with the monaural domain and DCN connectivity, but is explicitly stated as speculation requiring future testing. The manuscript appropriately distinguishes between demonstrated connectivity and inferred function, but the functional role of VIP neurons in auditory processing is not established by the current data.

results.result: A multidimensional approach incorporating molecular markers is essential for identifying neuron classes in the IC, as VIP neurons cannot be identified by morphology or physiology alone. This approach, successful in cerebral cortex for understanding circuit function, should be applied to identify remaining IC neuron classes.
results.evaluation: The claim that VIP neurons cannot be identified by morphology or physiology alone (C81) is well-supported by the data showing overlap with other IC neurons in these properties. The success of multidimensional classification in cortex (C79) is appropriately cited. The proposal for future work (C82) is reasonable given the demonstrated success of this approach for VIP neurons, though it represents a methodological recommendation rather than a result. This provides important context for interpreting the significance of the VIP neuron identification.

results.result: VIP neurons in the IC likely produce VIP peptide and may modulate the activity of postsynaptic targets through VIP signaling, as VIP receptors are expressed in target regions (MGB, SOC) and can potently affect neuronal excitability in other brain regions.
results.evaluation: The inference that IC VIP neurons produce VIP (C95) is reasonable based on high correlation (99.1%) between Cre expression and VIP immunostaining in cortex (C94), but this has not been directly demonstrated in the IC. The presence of VIP receptors in target regions (C96) and effects of VIP receptor activation in other brain areas (C97) are appropriately cited, but whether IC VIP neurons actually release VIP and modulate target neurons through VIP signaling (C98) remains speculative. This represents an important hypothesis for future testing but is not demonstrated by the current data.
